answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: From Cicero’s courtroom oration Pro Plancio (§80, delivered 54 BC). The Latin — “Haec enim est una virtus non solum maxima, sed etiam mater virtutum omnium reliquarum” — is authentic; this exact English wording is the condensed rendering in C. T. Ramage’s Great Thoughts from Latin Authors (1884).

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: 54 BC, in Cicero’s defense of Gnaeus Plancius
“Haec enim est una virtus non solum maxima, sed etiam mater virtutum omnium reliquarum.”
C. T. Ramage, Great Thoughts from Latin Authors (1884), p. 32

source.excerpt: In truth, O judges, while I wish to be adorned with every virtue, yet there is nothing which I can esteem more highly than the being and appearing grateful. For this one virtue is not only the greatest, but is also the parent of all the other virtues.
trail: The original is Cicero, Pro Plancio §80 (54 BC): “Haec enim est una virtus non solum maxima, sed etiam mater virtutum omnium reliquarum” — confirmed with the Yonge translation on Perseus ↗.

This exact English wording — “A grateful mind is not only the greatest of virtues, but the parent of all the other virtues” — is listed in Wikiquote’s sourced Cicero section ↗ as quoted in C. T. Ramage, Great Thoughts from Latin Authors (1884), p. 32.

A slightly different later rendering, “Gratitude is not only the greatest of virtues, but the parent of all others,” is the form that dominates the modern internet — a paraphrase of the same passage, not a separate Cicero quote.
source.excerptNote: The C. D. Yonge translation of the fuller passage on Perseus ↗. The popular one-liner (“A grateful mind…”) is Ramage’s tighter 1884 rendering of the same Latin sentence — “a grateful mind” captures gratus animus.
source.rightsNote: Cicero’s Latin (54 BC) is long in the public domain, and the specific English wording comes from C. T. Ramage’s Great Thoughts from Latin Authors (1884) — published well before 1931, so that translation is public domain in the United States.

author.name: Marcus Tullius Cicero
author.heading: About Cicero
author.bio: Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC) was Rome’s greatest orator and a prolific writer on rhetoric, politics, and philosophy. The gratitude line comes from Pro Plancio, a defense speech he delivered in 54 BC on behalf of Gnaeus Plancius, who had once sheltered Cicero during his exile — giving the theme of gratitude a personal edge.

misattribution.heading: About the wording
misattribution.intro: The author is right — this really is Cicero. The wrinkle is the wording: the memorable one-liner is a translator’s compression of a longer Latin sentence, and it circulates in several slightly different English forms.

items.why: Cicero wrote a fuller sentence about “being and appearing grateful”; the crisp “A grateful mind is not only the greatest of virtues…” is Ramage’s condensed English rendering in Great Thoughts from Latin Authors (1884), p. 32 ↗, not a literal one-to-one quotation.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Cicero delivered Pro Plancio in 54 BC to defend Gnaeus Plancius, a magistrate accused of electoral corruption. Plancius had sheltered Cicero during his exile two years earlier, so when Cicero praises gratitude as the supreme virtue, he is also publicly repaying a debt.

In the surrounding lines he grounds the claim by arguing that gratitude underlies love of parents, loyalty to country, piety toward the gods, and true friendship — each of them, in his telling, a child of a grateful mind.
context.pull: “This one virtue is not only the greatest, but is also the parent of all the other virtues.”
